Analyses: Swabian Aurignacian

Description

This file enables analyses of feature values for sequences on Swabian Aurgnacian objects (entropy rate, TTR, repetition rate, unigram entropy) as a function of meta information (object type, volume, cave site, etc.).

Session Info

Give the session info (reduced).

Load Data

Load feature estimations with meta data for the Aurignacian mobile objects.

sign.data <- read.csv("~/Github/UpperPalCombinatorics/results/features/signBase_features.csv")
# select Aurignacian data
sign.data <- sign.data[sign.data$archaeological_unit == "Aurignacien", ]

Preprocessing

Add columns for object volume and dates.

# volume in cm^3 (mm multiplications divided by 1000)
sign.data$volume <- (sign.data$length_mm*sign.data$width_mm*sign.data$depth)/1000
sign.data$date <- as.numeric(substr(sign.data$date_bp_max, 1, 5)) # note that min dates are complete

Collapse Factors

Collapse some factors of meta information which are uncommon and/or related. Note that using the factor levels as is will lead to problems with model fitting, since there are sometimes very few data points per level.

# material: collapse manually
sign.data$material <- fct_collapse(sign.data$material,
             ivory = "ivory",
             antler = "antler",
             bone = "bone",
             other_level = "other")

# object_type: collapse manually
sign.data$object_type <- fct_collapse(sign.data$object_type,
             figurine_anthropomorph = c("figurine anthropomorph",
                          "plaquette"),
             # note: the "plaquette" is the so-called Adorant with an anthropomorph figure on it.
             figurine_zoomorph = grep('figurine zoomorph.', unique(sign.data$object_type), value = TRUE),
             tool = c("awl", "bâton percé",
                      "rod/bâton", "spatula/lissoir"),
             tube_flute = c("flute", "tube", "tube/flute"),
             personal_ornament = c("personal ornament"),
             other_level = "other")

Exclude certain levels of columns to check the robustness of results.

Sign Stats

Cave Sites

Get frequency counts for individual sign types per cave site.

# initialize dataframe to append results to
caveSigns.df <- data.frame(signs = character(0),
                             Freq = numeric(0), 
                             site_name = character(0))

for (site_name in unique(sign.data$site_name)){
  # get all cleaned codings per cave
  codings <- sign.data[sign.data$site_name == site_name, ]$coding_clean 
  # collapse to one sequence
  codings.collapsed <- paste(codings, collapse = "")
  # remove underscores
  codings.collapsed <- gsub("_", "", codings.collapsed)
  # split into individual signs
  signs <- unlist(strsplit(codings.collapsed, ""))
  # get data frame with frequency counts
  signs.df <- as.data.frame(table(signs))
  # order by frequency
  signs.df <- signs.df[order(-signs.df$Freq), ]
  # add column with site_name
  signs.df$site_name <- rep(site_name, nrow(signs.df))
  # append results to dataframe
  caveSigns.df <- rbind(caveSigns.df, signs.df)
}

Barplot for frequency counts per sign type and cave site.

caveSigns.barplot <- ggplot(caveSigns.df, aes(x = reorder(signs, Freq), 
                                          y = Freq, fill = signs)) +
  #ylim(0, 700) +
  geom_text(aes(label = signs), hjust = -1) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  facet_wrap(~site_name, ncol = 5) +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  coord_flip() +
  xlab("Sign Types") +
  ylab("Token Frequency")
#caveSigns.barplot

Statistical Model

Linear Models

We here fit linear models with feature values (e.g. entropy rates) as response variable, and meta information (e.g. volume, type of object, material etc.) as predictor variables. Alternatively, especially the number of different sign types could also be used as a response, as this is highly correlated with the entropy rate. However, model checking reveals that some of the assumptions of linear regression (e.g. normality of residuals) are not met in this case. Some of the predictors are numerical (e.g. volume) while others are categorical (e.g. material, object_type). Arguably, a linear multiple regression model is appropriate since each object and its respective sequence of signs can be seen as an independent data point. Of course, it is theoretically possible that the same paleolithic person has produced a subset of the objects. However, there is no way of knowing this with certainty. Hence, there is no clear evidence for “repeated measures” as in controlled experiments with humans (with subjects and items, cf. Baayen, 2014) – which would require a mixed-effects structure.

# linear model with statistical feature values as response
linear.model <- lm(feature.values ~ object_type + material +
                   + volume + date + preservation + site_name, 
               data = sign.data)
AIC(linear.model) 
## [1] 147.0407

Model Summary

summary(linear.model)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = feature.values ~ object_type + material + +volume + 
##     date + preservation + site_name, data = sign.data)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -0.85971 -0.23566 -0.04573  0.22963  0.90795 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                                     Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)                        1.769e+00  5.055e-01   3.500  0.00058 ***
## object_typefigurine_anthropomorph  2.839e-01  1.553e-01   1.828  0.06907 .  
## object_typefigurine_zoomorph       3.107e-01  1.055e-01   2.944  0.00365 ** 
## object_typetube_flute             -2.206e-01  9.620e-02  -2.294  0.02291 *  
## object_typepersonal_ornament      -3.452e-01  1.251e-01  -2.760  0.00635 ** 
## object_typeother                  -9.939e-02  7.036e-02  -1.413  0.15941    
## materialbone                      -1.402e-01  1.589e-01  -0.882  0.37888    
## materialivory                     -1.822e-01  1.530e-01  -1.191  0.23514    
## materialother                     -4.056e-01  2.799e-01  -1.449  0.14900    
## volume                             2.760e-03  1.827e-03   1.510  0.13262    
## date                              -1.760e-05  1.458e-05  -1.207  0.22899    
## preservationcomplete              -1.222e-01  1.366e-01  -0.895  0.37207    
## preservationfragmented            -1.788e-01  8.652e-02  -2.067  0.04008 *  
## site_nameHohle Fels                1.261e-01  9.215e-02   1.368  0.17290    
## site_nameVogelherd                 2.272e-02  7.671e-02   0.296  0.76736    
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.3333 on 189 degrees of freedom
##   (7 observations deleted due to missingness)
## Multiple R-squared:  0.2906, Adjusted R-squared:  0.238 
## F-statistic:  5.53 on 14 and 189 DF,  p-value: 7.065e-09

Interpretation: In the model summary above, the reference level for object_type is “tools”, i.e. the residue category. Hence, the entropy rates of sign sequences found on anthropomorph figurines are on average higher than the ones found on objects classified as tools. A similar effect occurs for zoomorph figurines which also carry more information than tools on average. Inversely, entropy rates of sequences on tubes and flutes as well as personal ornaments are somewhat lower than on tools. There is no clear effect of the volume of an object on the entropy rate. There is no clear effect of the age of an object (c. 30 000 to 40 000 years old) either. Lastly, fragmented objects tend to have lower entropy rate than ``almost complete’’ ones. The details of the results (e.g. p-values) change for different versions of preprocessing (i.e. including and excluding certain data points), but the overall trends are similar. In particular, the entropy rate of sign sequences on zoomporph figurines is robustly higher than for the reference level of tools.

Checking of Model Assumptions

check_model(linear.model)

Write to file.

png(filename = file.path("~/Github/UpperPalCombinatorics/figures/", "modelCheckingPlot.png"), 
    width = 10, height = 10, units = "in", res = 300)
check_model(linear.model)
dev.off()
## png 
##   2

Shapiro-Wilk Test for Normality of Residuals

shapiro.test(rstandard(linear.model))
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  rstandard(linear.model)
## W = 0.99351, p-value = 0.514

Interpretation: There is a slight deviation from homogeneity of variance for the residuals (upper right panel), though this is due to just one or two data points deviating for the highest fitted values. There are no overly influential observations, and no collinearity between predictors (middle panels). There is a slight positive skew visible in the distribution of the residuals (lower panels). However, the Shapiro-Wilk test for normality gives a p-value > 0.05, meaning that the distribution does not significantly deviate from the expectation of a normal distribution (null hypothesis).

                     "Preservation: fragmented" = "preservationfragmented",
                     "Site name: Hohle Fels" = "site_nameHohle Fels",
                     "Site name: Vogelherd" = "site_nameVogelherd"))
## Loading required namespace: broom.mixed
#coefficient.plot

Sequence plot

# exclude "other" category (otherwise the sequence plot is overcrowded)
sign.data.modified <- sign.data[sign.data$object_type != "other", ] 
# take subsample as otherwise the sequence plot is overcrowded
sign.data.subsample <- sample_n(sign.data.modified, 50)
# get feature values for subsample
feature.values.modified <- get(feature.name, sign.data.modified)
feature.values.subsample <- get(feature.name, sign.data.subsample)

# create plot
sequence.plot <- ggplot(sign.data.subsample, aes(x = feature.values.subsample, 
                                                y = reorder(paste(coding_clean, object_id, sep = "  "), 
                                                            feature.values.subsample, mean), 
                                   size = volume, color = object_type)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  ylab("") +
  xlab(paste("Feature Values ", "(", feature.name, ")", sep = "")) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
sequence.plot
## Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

Density plot

density.plot <- ggplot(sign.data.modified, aes(x = feature.values.modified, 
                                               y = fct_reorder(object_type, feature.values.modified), 
                      fill = object_type, color = object_type)) +
  geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.5, scale = 1, quantile_lines = T, 
                      quantiles = 2, color = "white") +
  geom_point(shape = 124, alpha = 0.9, size = 3) +
  ylab("Object type") +
  xlab(paste("Feature Values ", "(", feature.name, ")", sep = "")) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
density.plot
## Picking joint bandwidth of 0.153

Combine figures.

model.plot <- ggarrange(sequence.plot,               # First column with sequence plot
          ggarrange(density.plot, coefficient.plot, 
                    ncol = 1, labels = c("B", "C")), # Second column with density and coefficient plot
          ncol = 2, 
          labels = "A",
          widths = c(2,1)                            # Relative widths of panels
          ) 
model.plot

Safe figure to file.

ggsave("~/Github/UpperPalCombinatorics/figures/modelPlot_Aurignacian.pdf", 
       model.plot, dpi = 300, width = 15, height = 8, device = cairo_pdf)
